Original source account: For the homogeneous one-dimensional constant-coefficient real system q_t + A q_x = 0, assume A has real eigenvalues and a corresponding basis of m eigenvectors. The source states that every vector has a unique expansion in this basis and that this yields a decomposition into waves, each propagating at the signed speed equal to its corresponding eigenvalue. The acoustic example has speeds −c and +c, representing leftward and rightward waves. The general decomposition is explained further by a reference to Chapter 3; the attached passage does not specify a solution regularity class or a general component formula. [Printed p. 1, (1.1); printed p. 2, acoustic scalar equations and directional interpretation; printed p. 3, opening paragraph.]
assumptions: The governing equation is the homogeneous, one-dimensional, constant-coefficient linear system q_t + A q_x = 0. [Printed p. 1, equation (1.1) and surrounding text; printed p. 3 explicitly refers back to system (1.1).]
The system is hyperbolic in the source's stated sense: A has real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors. [Printed p. 3, opening paragraph.]

The selected claim concerns the constant-coefficient system (1.1), as explicitly identified in its enclosing paragraph. The later conservation-law equation and variable flux Jacobian are introduced separately. [Printed p. 3, opening paragraph and section 1.1, equations (1.8)–(1.9).]
The two acoustic combinations satisfying scalar equations serve as the preceding model for the general wave decomposition. [Printed p. 2, formulas after (1.6); printed p. 3, opening sentence.]
The source distinguishes wave propagation speed from material particle velocity: acoustic waves can travel much faster than the material particles. [Printed p. 2, opening paragraph.]
